topics.title: What is the use() hook?
topics.html:
• Reads a Promise or Context. Unlike other hooks, can be called conditionally and inside loops.
  • Promise: integrates with Suspense — component suspends until resolved.
  • Context: like useContext but conditional-safe.
function Comments({ commentsPromise }: { commentsPromise: Promise<Comment[]> }) {
  const comments = use(commentsPromise); // suspends until resolved
  return <ul>{comments.map(c => <li key={c.id}>{c.text}</li>)}</ul>;
}
function Page() {
  const commentsPromise = api.getComments();
  return <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Comments commentsPromise={commentsPromise} /></Suspense>;
}
💬 Say it like this

use() is special — it's the only hook that can go inside an if block or a loop. When you pass it a Promise, the component suspends until it resolves, and the nearest Suspense boundary shows a fallback.

I reach for React Query for client-side caching and refetching. use() is more for Server Components or one-shot promises passed from a framework.

When use() vs useQuery?
use() for Server Components and one-shot framework promises. React Query for client-side caching, refetching, mutations, retries.

topics.title: useActionState — replaces isLoading/setError boilerplate.
topics.html:
async function loginAction(_prevState: State, formData: FormData) {
  try {
    const user = await api.login({ email: formData.get("email") as string, password: formData.get("password") as string });
    return { ok: true, user };
  } catch (e: any) { return { ok: false, error: e.message }; }
}
function LoginForm() {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(loginAction, { ok: false });
  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="email" type="email" required />
      <input name="password" type="password" required />
      <button disabled={isPending}>{isPending ? "Signing in..." : "Sign in"}</button>
      {!state.ok && state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}
💬 Say it like this

Before React 19, every form had this boilerplate: const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false), set it before the request, clear it in finally. useActionState replaces all of that. You give it an async action function and an initial state, it gives you back the current state, the form action to attach, and an isPending boolean. Much cleaner.

MEDIUM Q — useFormStatus

function SubmitButton({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();
  return <button disabled={pending}>{pending ? "Loading..." : children}</button>;
}
// Any form can drop <SubmitButton>Save</SubmitButton> inside it.

topics.title: useOptimistic — immediate UI update during async action.
topics.html:
function Likes({ post }: { post: Post }) {
  const [optimisticLikes, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
    post.likes,
    (current, action: "like" | "unlike") => current + (action === "like" ? 1 : -1)
  );
  async function toggleLike() {
    addOptimistic(post.liked ? "unlike" : "like");
    await api.toggleLike(post.id); // server state takes over when done
  }
  return <button onClick={toggleLike}>{optimisticLikes} likes</button>;
}
💬 Say it like this

Optimistic updates are when you update the UI immediately, before the server responds, assuming the request will succeed. useOptimistic makes this clean — call addOptimistic to show the instant update, fire the API call, and when it completes the real server state takes over. If the request fails, it rolls back.

topics.title: What is the React Compiler? What is a bail-out?
topics.html:
• A Babel plugin that builds a dependency graph per function and generates memoization code. Replaces most manual useMemo/useCallback/React.memo.
  • Bail-out: when a pattern is too complex to analyse safely, compiler silently skips the function — no error, no warning. Code still works, just not optimised.
  • ESLint (eslint-plugin-react-compiler) only catches Rules of React violations. A bail-out from unsupported syntax is an internal compiler decision — ESLint never sees it.
  • Verify: run Babel directly, check whether compiler-runtime c appears in output for that function.

HARD Q — 3 patterns that cause bail-outs.

// Pattern 1 — Mutating ref.current in render
const ref = useRef(startFn);
ref.current = startFn; // ✗ BAIL-OUT — side-effect in render
useEffect(() => { ref.current = startFn; }); // ✓ COMPILES

// Pattern 2 — await with optional chaining inside try-catch
try {
  const result = await fn();
  await result.setActive?.({ session: result.createdSessionId }); // ✗ BAIL-OUT
} catch {}
// ✓ Fix: explicit if
const result = await fn();
if (result.setActive) { await result.setActive({ session: result.createdSessionId }); }

// Pattern 3 — Deeply nested optional chains in async context
// Any: multiple async calls + deeply nested ?. + exception handling
TIP: 'The compiler is conservative by design. When it can't prove memoization is safe it skips the function — working code, no optimisation. No warning. Verify by inspecting Babel output.'
Should I delete all useMemo/useCallback after enabling the compiler?
No. Verify compilation first (Babel output). Keep them where referential stability matters — useEffect deps, third-party hook APIs, custom hooks exposing stable refs.
Does following Rules of React guarantee compilation?
No — necessary but not sufficient. A rule-compliant function can still bail out from unsupported syntax. Rules = ESLint. Compilation = Babel output.
💬 Say it like this

The React Compiler is a Babel plugin that adds memoization for me, so I do not have to write useMemo and useCallback by hand.

The part people miss is the bail-out. If the compiler cannot prove that memoizing a component is safe, it just skips that function. There is no error and no warning — the code works, it is simply not optimised. So I do not delete all my manual memoization blindly; I check the Babel output first to see if the component was really compiled.

topics.title: What else shipped in React 19 that you'd actually use day to day?
topics.html:
• ref is a normal prop — forwardRef is no longer needed for function components (it still works, and is on the deprecation path). Refs can also return a cleanup function.
  • <Context> as a provider — render <ThemeContext value={x}> directly, no .Provider.
  • Form actions — <form action={fn}>, plus formAction on buttons. React handles pending state and resets the form on success.
  • Document metadata — <title>, <meta>, <link> rendered anywhere in the tree get hoisted into <head>. No more react-helmet.
  • Resource preloading — preload, preinit, prefetchDNS, preconnect from react-dom to start fetches before render needs them.
  • Better errors — hydration mismatches now show a diff instead of two useless warnings; onCaughtError / onUncaughtError root options for reporting.
  • Stylesheet and async script support — precedence-ordered stylesheets, deduplicated async scripts.
// ref as a prop + cleanup
function Input({ ref, ...rest }: { ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement> }) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...rest} />;
}
<div ref={(node) => { observer.observe(node); return () => observer.unobserve(node); }} />

// metadata hoisted from anywhere in the tree
function ProductPage({ p }: { p: Product }) {
  return (<>
    <title>{p.name}</title>
    <meta name="description" content={p.summary} />
    <ProductView product={p} />
  </>);
}
💬 Say it like this

Apart from the Actions APIs, the changes I notice every day are small and practical. Ref is a normal prop now, so forwardRef disappears from my components. Context is rendered directly, without .Provider. And title and meta tags can be written inside any component — React moves them into the head, so I do not need a library like react-helmet any more.

topics.title: React 19.2 — Activity, useEffectEvent, and why they exist.
topics.html:
• <Activity mode="hidden"> — keep a subtree mounted but visually hidden, with its effects torn down and its state preserved. The proper answer to "keep the previous tab alive" and to pre-rendering the next screen without paying for it.
  • useEffectEvent — extracts non-reactive logic out of an effect. You read the latest props/state inside it, but it doesn't become a dependency, which kills the "I put it in a ref to avoid re-subscribing" hack.
  • Performance Tracks in Chrome DevTools — React's own scheduling and component timings on the browser timeline.
  • Partial Pre-rendering primitives and batched Suspense reveals in SSR — fewer layout jumps when several boundaries resolve close together.
// The classic bug: the effect re-subscribes every time theme changes
useEffect(() => {
  const c = createConnection(roomId);
  c.on("connected", () => showToast("Connected!", theme));   // theme is reactive → dep
  c.connect();
  return () => c.disconnect();
}, [roomId, theme]);            // ← reconnects on a theme switch. Wrong.

// Fix: the non-reactive part becomes an effect event
const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => showToast("Connected!", theme));
useEffect(() => {
  const c = createConnection(roomId);
  c.on("connected", onConnected);
  c.connect();
  return () => c.disconnect();
}, [roomId]);                   // ← reconnects only when the room changes
💬 Say it like this

useEffectEvent solves a very common problem: an effect needs to read a current value, but it should not run again when that value changes. Before, people either left the value out of the dependency array or hid it in a ref. Now that part lives in an effect event and the dependency list stays correct. Activity is for keeping the state of a hidden part of the tree without running its effects — for example a tab the user may come back to.

Which React version should you claim to know?
19 is the current major (19.2 line, patches through 2026); the React Compiler went stable 1.0. Saying "we're on 19, using Actions and the compiler in a couple of packages" is a stronger answer than listing every API.
